title: Room-temperature near-infrared optical readout of triplet spin states integrated in carbon nanotubes towards quantum sensing
authors: J. Alejandro de Sousa, Ilias Vandevenne, Jana Nikolić, Tuur Boonen, Etienne Goovaerts, Sofie Cambré
abstract: Optically addressable electron spin qubits that function at room temperature and under ambient conditions are essential for advancing quantum sensing. Solid state defect platforms offer robust spin-photon interfaces but lack precise defect positioning and electronic tunability. Molecular spin qubits enable bottom up chemical design yet suffer from limited photostability. Here, we introduce para-halophenyl (-Cl, -Br and -I) quantum defects in (6,5) single wall carbon nanotubes that trap triplet excitons with a spin-photon interface that is operable under ambient, room temperature conditions. These defects were shown to emit in the near infrared within the biological transparency window, and their placement on the nanotube surface provides nanoscale proximity to target environments. The deep optical traps formed by the defects yield exceptional photostability. Here, we demonstrate optical initialization and readout of these triplet states at room temperature, provide proof of principle sensing of paramagnetic molecules, and highlight potential for on chip detection. Together, these results establish SWCNT defects as a promising new platform for future quantum sensing.
summary: This paper reports on using engineered halogen-functionalized defects in single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) as robust, room-temperature quantum spin qubits. By performing ODMR spectroscopy, the authors demonstrate optical control and readout of triplet spin states. This establishes SWCNTs as a promising, scalable solid-state platform for ambient quantum sensing.
main_problem: The central goal is to develop optically addressable electron-spin qubits that function robustly at room temperature and ambient conditions for advancing quantum sensing applications.
main_result: The researchers successfully demonstrated optical initialization and readout of triplet spin states in defect-functionalized SWCNTs at room temperature, showing potential for on-chip quantum sensing.
method: The study combines Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) spectroscopy measurements with detailed theoretical simulations using a spin Hamiltonian package.
model_or_system: The platform utilizes para-halophenyl quantum defects ($	ext{-Cl}$, $	ext{-Br}$, $	ext{-I}$) incorporated into (6,5) single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) to trap triplet excitons. These defects provide a stable spin-photon interface operable under ambient conditions.
key_observables: ODMR contrast ($\Delta P_L / P_L$), microwave resonance dips, and temperature/power dependence of the spin signals.
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, near-infrared emission (biological window), and the spin Hamiltonian parameters ($g$-tensor, Zero-field splitting parameters $D, E$).
main_assumptions: The negative ODMR contrast assignment relies on the assumption that $	ext{sp}^3$-defects yield states with their Z-axis parallel to the CNT axis; furthermore, room-temperature observations are considered 'conservative' due to potential laser-induced heating.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate ODMR spectra showing dependence on halogen substitution, defect density, magnetic field orientation, temperature, and external molecule concentration (e.g., TEMPO).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform and initial room-temperature measurements to detailed modeling using spin Hamiltonians, followed by systematic investigation of temperature, power, and external analyte interactions (like TEMPO).
why_interesting: This work bridges solid-state defect physics, quantum optics, and sensing, providing a concrete, scalable solid-state platform for quantum information processing that operates outside cryogenic environments.
